lesson.title: Transposition
lesson.summary: Transposing moves every note by the same interval; transposing instruments read music written higher or lower than it sounds.

section.title: Transposing by an interval
section.p: To transpose music is to move every note up or down by the same interval. The melody, its rhythm and its intervals stay the same; only the pitch level, and usually the key, change. Singers transpose songs to suit their range, and players transpose parts for instruments that read in another key.

Each note must move by exactly the same interval, with the right number and the right quality. Up a major second, C becomes D and E becomes F#. Spelling a note enharmonically, as Gb instead of F#, would change the letter distance and so the interval.

worked.title: Transpose a melody up a major second

step.p: This melody is in F major. Its fourth note, B, is raised by a natural sign: it lies an augmented fourth above the tonic.

figure.staff: F4/q A4/q G4/q B4/q | C5/h A4/h |.

step.p: Transpose the key first. A major second above F is G, so the new key is G major, with one sharp.
Move every note up one letter, a major second: F to G, A to B, G to A, C to D. The raised B becomes a raised C: C#, again an augmented fourth above the tonic.

section.p: An accidental in the original does not always become the same accidental in the transposition. What stays the same is its effect: a note raised in the old key is raised in the new key, whether by a sharp, a natural or a double sharp.

check.prompt: What is E4 transposed up a minor third?
check.explanation: A third spans three letters: E, F, G. E–G is three half steps, a minor third. G#4 is a major third above, and F##4 sounds like G4 but is written as a second.

section.title: Transposing instruments
section.p: Some instruments, the transposing instruments, sound at a different pitch from the written note. The note in the part is the written pitch, which the player reads and fingers; the note that actually sounds is the sounding pitch, or concert pitch.

Such an instrument is named after the note that sounds when it plays a written C. A clarinet in Bb playing a written C5 sounds Bb4, a major second lower. To write for it, transpose the concert pitch up a major second.

list.li: Clarinet in Bb, trumpet in Bb, soprano saxophone: sound a major second lower than written.
Clarinet in A: sounds a minor third lower.
Horn in F, English horn: sound a perfect fifth lower.
Alto saxophone, in Eb: sounds a major sixth lower.

Tenor saxophone, in Bb: sounds a major ninth lower, an octave and a major second. The bass clarinet in Bb also sounds a major ninth lower when its part is written in the treble clef, as is usual today; parts written in the bass clef sound a major second lower.
Piccolo: sounds an octave higher. Guitar and double bass: sound an octave lower.

section.p: The key signature moves with the notes. Each sharp added or flat removed counts as one step towards the sharp side. Parts for instruments in Bb are two steps sharper than concert pitch: concert C major becomes D major, and concert F major, with one flat, becomes G major, with one sharp. Parts for instruments in F are one step sharper, and parts for instruments in Eb three steps. Horn parts in older music are often written without a key signature, with accidentals instead.

Most orchestral scores are transposed scores, with every part as its player reads it. Many modern scores, however, are printed in C, at concert pitch, so that the conductor reads every part as it sounds: a concert score. The players' parts are still transposed.

check.prompt: A trumpet in Bb plays a written D5. Which note sounds?
check.explanation: A Bb instrument sounds a major second lower than written. A major second below D5 is C5. Bb4 is what sounds for a written C5.

check.prompt: A horn in F plays a written C5. Which note sounds?
check.explanation: The horn in F sounds a perfect fifth lower than written: a written C sounds F, as its name says. A fifth below C5 is F4.

worked.title: Transpose a concert-pitch melody for clarinet in B flat

step.p: Start from the melody at concert pitch, in Eb major with three flats.

figure.staff: Eb4/q G4/q Bb4/q G4/q | Ab4/q F4/q Eb4/h |.

step.p: The clarinet sounds a major second lower than written, so its part must be written a major second higher than the sound.
Transpose the key: a major second above Eb is F. F major has one flat: two flats fewer than concert pitch, as for every instrument in Bb.
Move each note up a major second: Eb to F, G to A, Bb to C, Ab to Bb and F to G. Played on the clarinet, this part sounds exactly like the concert-pitch melody.

figure.staff: F4/q A4/q C5/q A4/q | Bb4/q G4/q F4/h |.
figure.caption: The clarinet part, at written pitch.

check.prompt: A piece is in Bb major at concert pitch. In which key is the alto saxophone part written?
check.explanation: The alto saxophone sounds a major sixth lower than written, so its part is written a major sixth higher. A major sixth above Bb is G: G major, with one sharp instead of two flats: three steps sharper, as for every instrument in Eb. C major is the key for an instrument in Bb.

check.prompt: A clarinet in A plays a written C5. Which note sounds?
check.explanation: The clarinet in A sounds a minor third lower than written, so a written C5 sounds A4, the note in its name.
